title: Design a Rate Limiter
description: Design a rate limiting system that protects APIs from abuse — covering algorithms, distributed challenges, and architectural placement.

segments.text: Today we're designing a rate limiter. It's the bouncer at the club door — deciding who gets in and who's been coming back too many times. Every major API uses one.

Why rate limit? To prevent abuse, protect resources, control costs, and ensure fair usage. Without it, one misbehaving client can starve everyone else. Think DDoS attacks or a buggy script hammering your API.
Let's start with the token bucket algorithm. Imagine a bucket that fills with tokens at a steady rate — like a faucet dripping water. Each request costs one token. Bucket empty? Request denied.

The beauty of token bucket is burst handling. If the bucket holds 10 tokens and refills at 1 per second, a client can burst 10 requests instantly, then sustain 1 per second after. Flexible and forgiving.
segments.thought_prompt: What if we want strict per-second limits with no bursts allowed?

segments.text: Fixed window counting divides time into fixed intervals — say, one-minute windows. Count requests per window. Simple to implement, but has a boundary problem: 100 requests at the end of one window plus 100 at the start of the next doubles your intended limit.

Sliding window fixes this. Instead of fixed boundaries, it tracks the weighted count across the current and previous windows. It smooths out boundary spikes while staying memory-efficient. Most production rate limiters use this.

Now the hard part — going distributed. If your API runs on multiple servers, each server needs the same view of request counts. Redis is the go-to solution. Store counters in Redis with INCR and EXPIRE commands for atomic, shared state.

But beware of race conditions. Two servers read the counter as 99 out of 100, both allow the request, and now you're at 101. Use Redis Lua scripts to make read-check-increment atomic. One round trip, no races.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens to rate limiting if Redis goes down?

segments.text: Where should the rate limiter live? At the API gateway, it catches abuse before it hits your services. Inside the application, you get finer-grained control per user or per endpoint. Many systems use both layers.

Good rate limiters communicate with clients. Return headers like X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After. This lets well-behaved clients back off gracefully instead of blindly retrying and making things worse.

Design for failure. If your rate limiter crashes, should you allow all traffic or deny all traffic? Most systems fail open — let requests through. A brief over-limit is better than a total outage for every user.
segments.thought_prompt: When might you want to fail closed instead of fail open?

segments.text: To recap: token bucket for flexibility, sliding window for precision, Redis for distributed state, Lua scripts for atomicity, and gateway placement for broad protection. A rate limiter is a small component with outsized impact on system reliability.
